turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, it's... I guess the main thing that brings me in today is that I just keep getting up when I'm really, absolutely supposed to stay put. It's becoming a real issue. 

I'm a private investigator, so you'd think my job is all action and running around, but there's actually a lot of sitting and consulting involved. And lately—well, maybe not just lately, but it's really getting obvious now—during client interviews, when they're sitting right across my desk explaining a really sensitive case, like a cheating spouse or a missing family member, I just stand up. I can't help it. I'll pace, or go check the blinds, or just stand by the door. 

And it's not just at work, either! I do some tutoring on the side for high school kids, and I cannot for the life of me just sit in the chair next to the student. I'm up, I'm walking to the kitchen for water, I'm leaning against the wall while they work out a math problem. Even at my book club! We meet on Tuesday nights at my friend's house, and everyone else is lounging on the sofas, having wine and discussing the chapters, and I'm the only one constantly popping up out of my seat. 

People are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen. My book club friends have started making little comments about it, and my clients probably think I'm not paying attention to them or that I'm trying to rush them out the door. Which isn't true at all, I hear every single word they say, but my body just... I can't stay anchored in the chair. It's getting embarrassing, honestly, and I just don't know why I can't force myself to stay seated like a normal person.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they constantly get up from their seat during client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club meetings when they are expected to remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in grade school, did you find it difficult to stay seated in your chair during class?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, grade school. Yes, absolutely. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my mother about this the other day—well, not about coming here, but just reminiscing, you know? She kept all my old report cards in this big, dusty accordion folder in her attic, and we were looking through them. And every single one of them, I swear, from first grade all the way through middle school, had the exact same comments from the teachers. They always said I was a bright girl, very capable, but that I just could not stay in my seat. Or wait my turn, for that matter! 

I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade—she had this little reading corner with beanbag chairs, and I would always end up migrating over there in the middle of a math lesson, or I’d be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or just walking to the back of the room to look at the class pet, which was a hamster named Barnaby. My mother still jokes about it. She always says, "You treated every classroom like a crime scene you had to pace through, looking for clues!" Which, I mean, is a little ironic now given my profession, but back then it was just... I don't know, I just felt this constant hum in my legs. Like if I didn't get up and move around, I was going to explode. 

And the teachers would get so frustrated! They’d say, "Please, just sit down for five minutes," and I’d try, I really would, but then before I even realized what I was doing, I was standing up again. It was like my body had a mind of its own. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new thing, this whole not-being-able-to-sit-still business. It’s been happening for as long as I can remember, really.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states she could not stay in her seat during class and would frequently get up to walk around the room.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling a 'constant hum' in her legs and feeling like she would explode if she didn't get up and move around, indicating severe restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient mentions that her teachers noted on her report cards that she could not wait her turn.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the physical restlessness and need to move, do you frequently find yourself struggling to maintain focus or making careless mistakes when you are performing tasks that require sustained mental effort?
turns.patient_response:
Focus? No, not really. Honestly, my focus is pretty sharp, which is probably why I'm good at what I do. I mean, when you're a private investigator, you have to be able to zero in on the details, right? You're combing through bank statements, or reviewing hours of surveillance footage, or reading through endless pages of court documents, and you really can't afford to make careless mistakes. If I miss a single transaction or a tiny discrepancy in a timeline, it could blow a whole case wide open—or, well, close it prematurely, I guess. 

So, no, I don't really struggle with that part of it. I can sit down—well, maybe not sit, like I said, I'll stand at my desk or pace around the room with the file in my hand—but mentally, I am completely locked in. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what I'm looking for, and I don't make those silly little errors that people talk about. Even when I'm tutoring the kids in math, I'm the one catching their dropped negative signs or misplaced decimals while I'm leaning against the whiteboard. 

It's actually kind of funny, because people always assume that if you're physically bouncing off the walls, your brain must be bouncing all over the place, too. But for me, it's almost like the movement helps me concentrate? Like, if my legs are doing something, my brain is free to just laser in on whatever puzzle I'm trying to solve. I don't find myself drifting off or staring blankly at the page. I'm very thorough, very detail-oriented. My clients actually praise me for how meticulous I am, which is nice to hear, especially when I'm feeling self-conscious about, you know, constantly getting up to adjust the thermostat or check the hallway during our meetings. But yeah, the mental effort part, the sustaining focus—that's never really been a problem for me. It's just the physical anchoring that I can't seem to manage.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions constantly getting up during meetings and standing or pacing instead of sitting at their desk.
symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes or 'silly little errors' in their work.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient states that sustaining focus has never been a problem and that they are 'completely locked in'.
symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient explicitly states that engaging in tasks requiring mental effort is not a problem for them.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient denies drifting off or losing their place, stating they can 'laser in' on tasks without being distracted.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself blurting out answers before questions have been completed, or interrupting others when they are speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, blurting things out... yeah. Yes, I do that. A lot, actually. It’s... well, it’s kind of a running issue with me, and I honestly feel terrible about it. 

I share a workspace with a few other investigators, including a couple of junior detectives who are just sort of getting their feet wet in the industry. Our office has these incredibly thin walls, so if I’m standing by my desk and I hear them out in the bullpen discussing a lead on a case—maybe they're trying to figure out how to track down a difficult witness or piece together a timeline—I just cannot stop myself. I will literally walk right out there and jump right into the middle of their sentence with a barrage of questions, or I'll just start rattling off unsolicited advice on how they need to run the background check or pull the property records. I don't wait to be asked for my input. I don't even knock on the door frame to announce myself! 

And it’s not just at work with the junior guys, either. It happens at my apartment building all the time. I'll be walking to the elevator or checking my mail, and if I hear a neighbor talking in the hallway to someone else—maybe they're complaining about a parking issue or a weird noise from the boiler room—I just insert myself right into their conversation. I'll start telling them exactly who they need to call or what city ordinance applies, completely unprompted. 

The worst part is that I don't even realize I'm doing it in the moment. It’s like my ears pick up on a problem or a puzzle being discussed, and my mouth just immediately takes over to solve it. It’s only afterward, when there's this awkward pause and they're staring at me because I just completely hijacked their private chat, that I realize I absolutely barged into someone else's conversation. I always have to backtrack and apologize, but it's like I just lack that internal filter that tells you to mind your own business. I get so eager to help or to get to the bottom of things that I completely bulldoze over normal social boundaries before my brain can catch up and tell me to keep my mouth shut.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly confirms that they blurt things out a lot in response to the doctor's question about blurting out answers.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes frequently barging into and hijacking the private conversations of junior detectives and neighbors without being asked.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find that you lose or misplace essential items like your keys, wallet, or important documents required for your work?
turns.patient_response:
Lose things? Oh, no. No, never. That is... well, that's just one area where I am absolutely rigid. I really don't lose my belongings. 

You see, when you're a private investigator, chain of custody and secure documentation are basically your entire livelihood. If I were to misplace a client's file, or lose a thumb drive with surveillance footage on it, it wouldn't just be an inconvenience, it would be a complete disaster. It could compromise a case, or violate confidentiality agreements, and I just refuse to let that happen. 

So I have systems. Very, very strict systems. When I walk into my apartment, for instance, there is a small brass bowl on the console table in the entryway—my sister actually brought it back for me from a trip to Morocco years ago, it's got this beautiful intricate etching on it—and my keys go into that bowl the absolute second I walk through the door. I don't set them on the kitchen counter, I don't leave them in my coat pocket, they go in the bowl. Every single time. It's practically muscle memory at this point. 

And my wallet is the exact same way. It lives in the interior zippered pocket of my leather messenger bag. I never just carry it around loose. If I take it out to buy a coffee, it goes right back into that specific pocket before I even step away from the register. 

As for work documents, I am borderline obsessive. I have a color-coded filing system at the office, and if I have to transport any sensitive paperwork between the office and my apartment, or to a client meeting, it goes into a waterproof, lockable briefcase. I actually had a colleague years ago—this was back when I was just starting out—who left a highly sensitive manila folder on the subway. Just set it on the seat next to him and walked off at his stop. Let me tell you, the fallout from that was catastrophic. He almost lost his license over it. I remember watching that happen and thinking, "Okay, that will absolutely never be me." 

So I think because my body is always moving, like I was saying earlier, I subconsciously realized a long time ago that I needed a foolproof system for my physical objects. Otherwise, yes, things probably would just fly right out of my pockets while I'm pacing around. But because I'm so hyper-aware of it, I know exactly where my keys, my wallet, my phone, and my files are at any given second. Actually, I'm usually the one finding things for the junior detectives in the office when they misplace their own notebooks! So no, losing things really isn't something I struggle with at all.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient notes that their body is 'always moving' and mentions 'pacing around', indicating constant physical activity.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies losing things, stating 'Oh, no. No, never' and describing strict systems they use to keep track of their belongings.
